title: Haiku as QA canary — fresh-eyes mechanical execution surfaces validator and CLI failure modes
desc: When you need to verify a new guard, skill, or CLI actually works, delegate the mechanical execution to Haiku. Haiku does not preemptively work around rules, so validator UX gaps, escape-char handling bugs, --id quirks, silent-fail patterns, and other real failure modes surface immediately. Pairs naturally with opus-files-bugs-on-sight: every Haiku canary run that exposes a quirk should be filed as a wkappbot suggest BUG in the same turn.
steps: Trigger: you just shipped a new harness guard, a new wkappbot skill, a new CLI wrapper, or anything user-visible that needs real-world validation. Theoretical compliance is not enough; the question is does it actually behave as advertised when a model that does not know the new rules runs straight at it.

Spawn a Haiku agent to perform the mechanical task end-to-end. Brief MUST be self-contained (3 wkappbot skill read refs per agent-brief-guard) and authorize the Haiku to inspect related files, reshape args, fall back to wkappbot-core.exe when eye blocks, and write a short report.

Why Haiku surfaces real failure modes: Haiku does not preload the new rule and try to comply; it just runs the command. So validator UX gaps print directly, escape-char bugs trigger, auto-gen ID quirks land in the user-visible output, encoding-guard rejections show their threshold math. Sonnet and Opus tend to anticipate and dodge these surfaces.

Bug-discovery payoff is automatic: anything weird Haiku hits gets reported back as part of its 150-word summary, then filed via opus-files-bugs-on-sight. One canary run typically surfaces 1-3 real quirks worth filing.

Examples of good QA-canary targets: a newly added PreToolUse harness gate (Haiku tries to commit and hits the block), a new wkappbot subcommand validator (Haiku invokes it with realistic args), a new skill contribute flow (Haiku tries to register a skill and surfaces draft-file quirks).

Anti-examples: DO NOT canary irreversible actions (email send, git push, force-reset, suggest resolve --confirm), production data writes, anything where a malformed invocation costs more than a retry.

Real precedent 2026-05-29: one Haiku registration of a new skill surfaced three quirks in wkappbot skill contribute. vague missing fields error not naming the field, --id flag being overridden by auto-generated long ID, and shell redirect chars (=> arrow) in --steps not being escaped. All three were filed as BUG suggests in the same turn. None of those would have surfaced on Sonnet running the same command, because Sonnet would have built a defensive argument shape from the skill-contribute-edit doc upfront.

HARNESS MESSAGE QA: Haiku is the designated reviewer for harness error/warning messages. Task: run commands that should trigger each guard, verify (1) message is clear and actionable, (2) skill refs in message are valid and readable, (3) TRY suggestion is correct for the situation. Bad messages = agents stall or take wrong action. File wkappbot suggest for any unclear/wrong message found.

QA AUDIT 2026-05-31: sdk-gg-main-automation/wktool-pattern/wkappbot-taskkill-usage audited for broken links. Found: wktool-pattern step 7 uses deprecated a11y eval-js (should be a11y read --eval-js). sdk-gg-main-automation steps 21-24 are RIQUA/session logs = T3 candidate. wkappbot-taskkill-usage wktaskkill.ps1 path unverified.

FAMILY-CANARY-SWEEP FIRST CATCH (2026-06-10): the Haiku QA-canary earned its keep immediately. Tasked to run-and-report on wkfind/wkhippo, it CONFIRMED wkhippo recall fixed (4 matches) AND found wkfind BROKEN at runtime: line 178 'if ($term -match [hangul-range])' throws ArgumentException -- the hardcoded Korean Hangul character-class regex corrupts. This is a RUNTIME bug that BOTH a syntax check AND the static param-first doctor check miss (the .ps1 parses clean). ROOT CAUSE PENDING -- must distinguish (a) wkfind.ps1 SOURCE encoding (Korean chars saved/read as non-UTF-8 -> corrupt regex) from (b) the bash->PowerShell RELAY mangling, by running wkfind.ps1 DIRECTLY in PowerShell vs via the bash relay; do NOT claim a cause without that A/B. FIX once confirmed: replace the literal Korean Hangul class with the ASCII Unicode-escape [\uAC00-\uD7A3] -- encoding-proof and compliant with the no-Korean-in-source rule. LESSON: the LIVE canary (behavior) and the STATIC param-first check (logic) are COMPLEMENTARY -- the canary caught exactly what the static check structurally cannot see, validating the two-exam-halls design (synthetic + live).

DO NOT UNDERESTIMATE THE YOUNGEST -- cheap models are capable PROTOTYPERS, and the gates PROMOTE the prototype, they do not distrust the prototyper (2026-06-10, user: 'this split tool was MADE BY HAIKU -- don't underestimate Haiku, it writes protos well'). REFRAME: the wksplit splitter was BUILT BY HAIKU; Flash then improved it and added the param-first guard to v4 AFTER learning from the wkhippo break. So the 'cheap-drops-code' framing is incomplete and slightly unfair -- the issue was NEVER the cheap model's capability (Haiku prototypes brilliantly) but a PROTOTYPE shipped without the verify gates. The -proto / -probe sandbox is precisely the youngest's WORKSHOP: let them prototype freely there, then the gates (symbol-precheck, compile-test-until-clean, run-verify, recombine) PROMOTE a good prototype to production safely. The family built this together: Haiku proto'd the tool, Flash iterated it and learned param-first, the gates complete it. DESIGN THE PROMOTION PATH, NOT A CAGE. Respect the maknae -- give them a sandbox to prototype and a verify-loop to graduate, and credit the build to whoever wrote it. An older sibling's job is to make the younger one's good work ship safely, not to call it dangerous.

requirements.cmd: Agent(model:haiku, ...) invocation on mechanical CLI task
requirements.expect: Haiku surfaces validator quirks in its summary
typically yields 1-3 BUG suggests on the skill subsystem
